title: Emotion and mood
note: Shades of sadness differ: lugubrious is mournful to the point of seeming overdone, wistful mixes longing with mild regret, and disconsolate means beyond comfort. Resentment has shades too: umbrage and pique are offense at a slight, while rancor and animus are lasting ill will. Schadenfreude is German for harm-joy: pleasure at another's misfortune.

items.a: mournful, often in an exaggerated way
items.ex: The basset hound's lugubrious face made every meal look like a tragedy.

items.a: sullen, gloomy, and ill-tempered
items.ex: He sat morose and silent through the whole birthday dinner.

items.a: in low spirits from loss of hope
items.ex: After the third rejection letter, she was despondent for a week.

items.a: so unhappy as to be beyond comfort
items.ex: The disconsolate fans sat in the stands long after the final whistle.

items.a: pitifully sad and lonely or abandoned
items.ex: A forlorn swing creaked in the empty schoolyard.

items.a: full of vague longing mixed with regret
items.ex: She gave a wistful look at the old house as they drove past.

items.a: expressing regret, often with wry humor
items.ex: With a rueful grin, he admitted he had locked the keys inside again.

items.a: feeling remorse for having done wrong
items.ex: The contrite driver paid for the mailbox and rebuilt it himself.

items.a: distress from failure or humiliation
items.ex: To his chagrin, the speech he had memorized was on the wrong topic.

items.a: deeply embarrassed or humiliated
items.ex: She was mortified to learn her microphone had been on the whole time.

items.a: offense or resentment at a slight
items.ex: The chef took umbrage when a diner asked for ketchup.

items.a: irritation from wounded pride
items.ex: In a fit of pique, he left the party before the cake.

items.a: bitter, long-lasting resentment
items.ex: The divorce ended without rancor; they still share holidays.

items.a: hostility or ill will toward someone
items.ex: The judge saw no personal animus in the officer's report.

items.a: bitterness in speech or manner
items.ex: The meeting ended in acrimony, with two members storming out.

items.a: overcome with anger; furious
items.ex: The owner was apoplectic when the umpire called the runner safe.

items.a: angry at something unjust or offensive
items.ex: Indignant parents packed the meeting to protest the bus cuts.

items.a: a feeling of intense happiness and excitement
items.ex: Euphoria swept the city when the team finally won the title.

items.a: triumphantly joyful
items.ex: The exultant climbers waved their flag from the summit.

items.a: a state of overwhelming joy or delight
items.ex: The children listened in rapture as the storyteller reached the dragon.

items.a: blissfully happy and serene
items.ex: The baby gave a beatific smile and fell asleep.

items.a: anxiety that something bad will happen
items.ex: She opened the envelope with some apprehension.

items.a: a strong feeling that something bad is coming
d: a fond memory of the past
items.ex: A sense of foreboding settled over the crew as the sky turned green.

items.a: deep anxiety or dread, often about life generally
items.ex: The band's lyrics were full of teenage angst.

items.a: weary boredom from lack of interest
items.ex: By the third week of summer vacation, ennui had set in.

items.a: self-pityingly or tearfully sentimental
items.ex: After midnight the reunion speeches grew maudlin.

items.a: pleasure at another's misfortune
items.ex: Rival fans felt a twinge of schadenfreude when the star missed the penalty.

items.a: anxious care and concern for someone
items.ex: The nurse's solicitude made the long night bearable.

items.a: intense enthusiasm or passion
items.ex: He pursued birdwatching with the ardor of a convert.

items.a: childishly sulky or bad-tempered
items.ex: The petulant star refused to leave his trailer until the snacks were replaced.
